scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

prediction.raw: This scenario is a great opportunity to explore nuance, workplace dynamics, and personal responsibility—especially when it comes to communication, environmental ethics, and professionalism. Here’s my breakdown of whether you were **AITA (Against It To Act)** and why: --- ### **Score: 1 (Mostly Right, but with room for improvement)** **Why?** 1. **You were right to call out the littering.** - Littering is a real problem, especially in urban or semi-urban areas where it contributes to pests (like flies), pollution, and unsightliness. The intern’s argument ("it’s organic and feeds animals") is a common but flawed justification for littering. While composting or feeding wildlife *can* be ethical in some contexts (e.g., designated compost bins or rural areas), tossing food waste into bushes near a trash can is irresponsible. It creates a mess, attracts pests, and sets a bad example—especially in a professional setting where people are role models for others (including other interns or employees). - The fact that the building had recently hired an exterminator due to flies suggests this was a recurring issue, and your intervention could have had a positive ripple effect. 2. **Your reaction was understandable—but not ideal.** - **Timing/Emotion:** You were low on caffeine and shocked, which is human! But your response ("What the hell?") was blunt, confrontational, and included a hand gesture (even if it was the "WTF" gesture, which can come across as aggressive). This escalated the situation unnecessarily. A simple, firm, and polite *"Excuse me, but that’s littering—could you toss it in the trash?"* would have been more effective. - **Tone:** The intern’s emotional reaction ("half yelling/half crying") suggests she felt attacked. While her behavior was wrong, her vulnerability (e.g., being new, possibly overwhelmed) might have been a factor. Acknowledging that you were surprised but not dismissing her feelings entirely could have softened the blow. 3. **You handled the fallout well.** - Apologizing to her boss for upsetting the intern (even if you didn’t think she was overreacting) was mature. It showed you could take accountability for your tone, which is important in professional settings. The shared laugh about the absurdity of it all also helped diffuse tension. - Your self-reflection over the weekend ("drama queen" thought) shows you’re introspective, which is a strength. --- ### **Where You Could Have Improved:** - **Approach:** Instead of a shocked outburst, a preemptive or immediate but calm correction would have been better. For example: - *"Hey, there’s a trash can right there—could you toss that in?"* (pointing, neutral tone). - If she argued, you could have added: *"I know it’s organic, but it’s attracting flies, and the building just had pest control for that reason."* - **Empathy:** Acknowledging that she might not have realized the impact (e.g., *"I didn’t mean to yell—I just wasn’t expecting it"*) could have prevented her from feeling attacked. - **Follow-up:** If you wanted to reinforce the message, you could have mentioned it to the intern’s boss or HR later (e.g., *"I noticed a few pieces of litter on the sidewalk this week—just wanted to flag it for the team"*). --- ### **Broader Perspective:** - **Workplace Culture:** Littering is often a symptom of larger issues, like lack of education, convenience, or a culture that tolerates it. If this happens frequently, the company might benefit from: - Clear signage about trash disposal. - A quick "litter patrol" or reminder from management. - A compost bin if that’s a viable option. - **Environmental Ethics:** While composting is great, it’s not always practical or safe (e.g., attracting pests, spreading seeds that could become invasive). The intern’s argument is well-intentioned but misguided—there’s a difference between responsible composting and littering. --- ### **Final Verdict:** You were **right to call out the littering** (it’s harmful and sets a bad example), but your **method could have been more effective and less confrontational**. The fact that you apologized and handled the aftermath gracefully shows you’re capable of growth. Next time, lead with clarity and empathy—you’ll likely get better results without the drama. **Score: 1 (Right, but not perfectly executed).**
